title: FSSAI Proposes Ban on Added Sugars in Infant Food for Babies Under Six Months
excerpt: A draft amendment published on October 16 would bar adding sucrose and fructose to products for infants up to six months, with 60 days for public comment before the rules can be finalised.
body:
• India's food regulator FSSAI has proposed a complete ban on adding sucrose and fructose to infant nutrition products intended for babies up to six months old.
  • The draft amendment to the 2020 infant nutrition regulations was published in the Gazette on October 16, 2026, and is open for objections and suggestions for 60 days before it can be finalised.
  • Under current rules, sucrose and fructose may still be added within prescribed limits when needed as a carbohydrate source; the draft would remove that allowance for the youngest infants only.
  • For parents: nothing changes on shop shelves yet — until the final rules are notified, check ingredient lists on products for babies under six months for sucrose or fructose if you want to avoid added sugars now.

India's food safety regulator has proposed banning the addition of sucrose and fructose to infant nutrition products intended for babies up to six months old, tightening the rules on added sugars during the first months of life.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) notified the draft Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Amendment Regulations, 2026, on Saturday, saying the changes would ensure infant products are formulated in line with age-appropriate nutritional requirements, with particular emphasis on minimising exposure to added sugars at the earliest stage. The draft was published in the Gazette of India on October 16, according to the health ministry statement reported by Mint.

What exactly would change

The existing Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, set nutritional composition, quality and safety standards for products intended for children from birth to 24 months. Under those rules, lactose and glucose polymers are the preferred sources of carbohydrates, while sucrose and fructose may be added only when required as a carbohydrate source and subject to prescribed limits.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2111441332896141553

The draft would end that limited allowance for the youngest age group. As the text of the draft notification puts it, a new proviso to Regulation 3(6) would state that sucrose and fructose shall not be added in products intended for infants up to the age of six months. The restriction covers added sucrose and fructose; it does not extend the ban to products for older infants, and as a draft it is not yet enforceable law.

"Sucrose and fructose shall not be added in the products intended for infants up to the age of 6 months."

— Draft FSSAI amendment to the Foods for Infant Nutrition Regulations

Why the regulator is acting now

FSSAI said the first six months of life are a critical period for healthy growth and development, making appropriate nutrition particularly important. The proposed restriction, it said, is intended to ensure products meet the needs of this age group without unnecessary added sugars, and to support broader public-health efforts on dietary risk factors linked to childhood obesity and related conditions. The initiative also complements established recommendations promoting exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months.

The proposal follows a controversy that put added sugar in Indian baby food under sustained scrutiny. In April 2024, a Swiss investigation found that Nestlé added sugar to Cerelac sold in India while offering sugar-free versions in Europe, according to Mint. Mint had also previously reported, on March 6, that the government was planning tighter rules.

What it means for makers and parents

If finalised, manufacturers would have to reformulate any product for infants under six months that currently uses sucrose or fructose within the permitted limits. The commercial stakes are not small: Mint, citing MarkNtel Advisors, valued India's baby food market at $1.16 billion in 2024 and projected it to reach $1.98 billion by 2030.

For parents in India and in the diaspora who buy Indian-made infant products, the practical position today is unchanged. The 2020 rules remain in force, with sucrose and fructose still permitted within limits. Anyone who wants to avoid those sugars for a baby under six months needs to read the ingredient list until the final amendment is notified.

What happens next

The draft, dated October 15 and issued as F. No. RCD-09002/3/2026-Regulatory-FSSAI, invites objections and suggestions from stakeholders — manufacturers, industry associations, health professionals and consumers — to the Chief Executive Officer, FSSAI, FDA Bhawan, Kotla Road, New Delhi. FSSAI will consider representations received within 60 days of the Gazette copies being made available to the public before deciding on the final regulations, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. Only after that process, and with the Central Government's approval, would the ban become binding.
